title: the ripple, the wave that carried me home by Christina Anderson at Pl...
transcript: Janice has a complicated relationship with water. It represents the activism her family became known for and the heaviness it imposed on their relationships. As a memory play, this piece chronicles her upbringing, which Janice recounts through the most pivotal moments in her parents’ fight to integrate the community's public swimming pools. A brief synopsis doesn't do justice to all the layers this play has to offer — it's a family story at its core, elevated by richly embedded commentary on history and selective memory. The entire cast is delightfully charismatic, with Alana Raquel Bowers at the center, giving a grounded and often understated performance as Janice. In the present, which is 1992 in this case, she's assured, but there's a sense of disillusionment that comes through very early on in the play. It's a compelling, though sometimes painful experience to learn how this armor grew, and I think the play, despite its specificity in plot and characters, has many relatable elements. I personally was moved by its exploration of “home” requiring a distinction between a place that houses you and a place that truly holds you. The production is rounded out by some incredible costume and wig design, gloriously tied to the multiple eras depicted. With a refreshingly vivid but subversive story packed with quiet gut punches, “the ripple, the wave that carried me home” is a piece I'll be thinking about for quite some time. It is running now at Playwrights Horizons.
